metadata.narrative: Compose a concise technical report sketching an experimental plan for deciding whether a modern vision-language model could stand in for human specialists when labeling medical images of skin lesions.
metadata.run_desc: aus_agent research harness (bedrock/au.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5): iterative hybrid dense+sparse ClimbMix search + document fetch, strict-JSON cited sentence answers.

answer.text: This report sketches an experimental plan for testing whether a modern vision-language model (VLM) such as GPT-4V could substitute for human dermatology specialists when labeling skin lesion images, drawing on prior AI-vs-clinician benchmarks, annotation-quality methodology, and fairness/regulatory considerations.
Dermatology is a strong test case because large curated archives (ISIC, HAM10000) already exist for benchmarking.
Esteva et al. fine-tuned a CNN on 129,450 images spanning 2,000+ diseases and showed it matched or exceeded 21 board-certified dermatologists on biopsy-proven skin cancer classification.
A later study pitted a CNN against 58 dermatologists, finding ~95% CNN accuracy versus 86.6% for humans, with higher sensitivity and fewer unnecessary excisions.
Other trials show narrower margins (e.g., CNN 72%/55.4% on two tasks vs. ~65–66%/53–55% for individual dermatologists), indicating gaps depend heavily on task design.
Directly testing multimodal LLMs, GPT-4V reached 85% accuracy differentiating melanoma from benign nevi versus 45% for LLaVA, though both showed color-related biases.
In a clinical-case retrieval task, GPT-4V correctly identified the true skin condition from images plus brief histories 85% of the time, improved further by multi-agent chain-of-thought framing.
Hypotheses: (H1) VLM labels achieve non-inferior agreement with an expert-consensus reference versus individual specialists; (H2) VLM accuracy is stable across skin tones and lesion subtypes.
Ground truth should come from a dermatopathologist consensus panel, since even human pathologists show only 25–72% concordance with a reference panel across the disease spectrum.
Datasets should be stratified by diagnosis, difficulty, and skin tone using public archives (ISIC, HAM10000, MClass-D) plus textbook/Dermnet images.
Skin-of-color cases should be oversampled and reported separately, since only ~30% of dermatology AI tools specifically target skin of color.
A multidimensional skin-color measure, rather than a simple light/dark scale, should characterize dataset composition and reveal hidden bias.

Comparators should include board-certified dermatologists, primary care physicians, and a domain-tuned model (e.g., LLaVA-Med) to separate generalist-VLM performance from specialty level and specialization.

A Northwestern experiment found unaided dermatologists 38% accurate and primary care physicians 19% accurate, with AI assistance raising accuracy 33% and 69% respectively, but widening skin-tone disparities among primary care users.
This motivates including human+VLM and VLM-alone arms to test replacement versus assistive roles.
Prompt design should use feature-conditioned prompts (holding ABCDE melanoma features constant) since GPT-4V and LLaVA diverge sharply under such conditioning.
Chain-of-thought and multi-agent prompting strategies improve multimodal diagnostic performance over naive prompting and should be a design factor.
Primary accuracy outcomes should use sensitivity, specificity, and AUC-ROC against the panel reference, per standard diagnostic-accuracy practice.
Reliability outcomes should include Cohen's/Fleiss' kappa comparing VLM labels to specialists and consensus, the standard chance-corrected agreement measure.
Calibration (confidence vs. correctness) should also be reported, since overconfident inaccurate models are risky in high-stakes diagnosis.
Sample size/power should be calculated a priori, and reporting should follow the STARD 30-item checklist for transparency.
Cost/scalability should be benchmarked, since crowdsourced non-experts reached ~76% pixel-level agreement with experts on lesion delineation at much lower cost.
A human-in-the-loop framework, where the VLM proposes labels for specialist review, should be tested as an intermediate deployment mode given known LLM mislabeling risks.
Explainability should be assessed using Grad-CAM/saliency-style analogues or feature-justification prompts, noting these aid interpretation but don't prove correct reasoning.
Failure modes should be logged qualitatively (color bias, hallucinations, complex-reasoning errors), consistent with reported GPT-4V limitations.
Robustness tests should include perturbed inputs (decolorized images, annotations), since LLaVA misread annotation marks as sunburn while GPT-4V did not.
Regulatory framing matters: FDA cleared 91 AI/ML medical devices in 2022 via 510(k)/De Novo pathways, implying similar prospective validation would likely be needed for specialist-replacing claims.
Given documented skin-of-color and primary-care-bias disparities, any non-inferiority conclusion must include subgroup reporting rather than pooled accuracy alone.

Overall, the plan combines a stratified, bias-aware dataset, consensus reference standard, multiple comparator arms, structured/chain-of-thought prompting, STARD-compliant metrics and kappa agreement, calibration/explainability analysis, and cost benchmarking to responsibly assess VLM substitution for specialist labeling.
